text:
Key Concepts

saving result in R
result <- filter(counties, population > 5000)


packages
install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)


Data frames and dplyr
Main verbs: - filter() — choose rows based on conditions. - select() — choose columns. - mutate() — add or modify computed columns. - arrange() — sort rows; use desc() for descending order. - group_by() + summarize() — calculate statistics by group, similar to SQL aggregation.


Pipelines
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(name, moe_pct)


Getting ACS data
library(tidycensus)

data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c("VARIABLE_ID_1", "VARIABLE_ID_2"),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2014,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


GEOIDs
Treat GEOIDs as strings, not numbers, so leading zeros are preserved. Typical components: - State: 2 digits - County: 3 digits - Census tract: 6 digits - Block group: 1 additional digit when applicable A state + county + tract GEOID is usually 11 digits.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.]
Among California counties, Alpine and Sierra have the greatest relative uncertainty in their median age estimates. Alpine County has an estimated median age of 41.1 years and a margin of error (MoE) of 4.8 years (11.68% of the estimate). Sierra County has an estimated median age of 56 years and a MoE of 5 years (8.93%). Both are measured less precisely than other counties.
Using relative MOE cutoffs of 0.5% and 1%, the 16 high-confidence counties average roughly 1,711,758 residents, compared with 25,185 for the 16 low-confidence counties. The 26 moderate-confidence counties average 440,450. This pattern reflects how the ACS works: it surveys a sample of residents, and smaller counties yield fewer observations, so their estimates carry more uncertainty.
Suppose a state agency used median age to prioritize funding for older-adult services. An underestimated median age might cause a county to miss support; an overestimate might divert funding from communities that need it. Alpine and Sierra would be especially exposed to such errors. Agencies should weigh MoE alongside point estimates — and recognize that median age alone does not capture the number of older residents who need services.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Optional challenges - For those craving more
text:
Optional challenges - For those craving more
Using 2023 ACS five-year estimates, I compared the precision of median age estimates for Los Angeles County and its census tracts. The county’s relative MOE was 0.26%, while the median relative MOE across 2,477 valid tracts was 10.12%. Another 21 tracts were excluded for missing estimates.
With reliability thresholds at 5% and 10%, 181 tracts (7.31%) fell into high confidence, 1,037 (41.87%) into moderate, and 1,259 (50.83%) into low confidence.
A precise county estimate does not guarantee equally precise estimates at the tract level. Smaller areas yield fewer survey observations and more uncertainty. Agencies directing older-adult services to specific neighborhoods should check tract-level MOEs rather than relying on county precision alone.

title: Week 3: Visulaization
text:
Key Concepts

Anscombe’s Quartet
The four datasets have the same or nearly identical mean x, mean y, correlation, and regression line, but very different distributions when plotted.


How to Build a ggplot

Step 1: Assign an object and create a blank canvas
p <- ggplot(data)

# You can also start without specifying data
p <- ggplot()


Step 2: Define aesthetic mappings
aes() maps data to visual properties such as position and color.

Inside aes(): map a variable or category to a visual property.
Outside aes(): set a visual property to a fixed value.

# Map the category "blue" to color.
# This creates a legend labeled "blue";
# it does not necessarily make the points blue.
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct, color = "blue") +
  geom_point()

# Set all points to blue
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")

# Color points according to the city variable
ggplot(df, aes(x = income, y = rent)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = city))


Step 3: Choose a geometry



Function
Purpose




geom_histogram()
Show the distribution of a variable


geom_point()
Show the relationship between two variables


geom_boxplot()
Compare distributions across groups


geom_col()
Compare values across groups


geom_line()
Show changes over time


geom_errorbar()
Display uncertainty



p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = income, y = rent, color = city)) +
  geom_point()
The + operator adds layers or other plot components.



ACS Error and Reliability

Standard Error (SE)
For an ACS margin of error reported at the 90% confidence level:
\[
SE = \frac{MOE}{1.645}
\]


Coefficient of Variation (CV)
\[
CV = \frac{SE}{\text{Estimate}} \times 100%
\]
CV thresholds from the class notes:



CV Level
Range
Interpretation




Low
< 15%
High reliability


Medium
15%–30%



High
> 30%
High sampling error





Uncertainty in Derived Estimates
When calculating sums, proportions, or ratios, account for uncertainty in the original estimates. Both the numerator and denominator may have sampling error.








Function
Purpose
Example




moe_sum()
Calculate the MOE of a sum
Add populations across several areas


moe_prop()
Calculate the MOE of a part-to-whole proportion
Population in poverty ÷ population for whom poverty status is determined


moe_ratio()
Calculate the MOE of a general ratio
Number of jobs ÷ number of housing units





Changes Over Time
When comparing ACS multiyear estimates, use periods with non-overlapping years.
Convert each period’s MOE to its standard error:
\[
SE_1 = \frac{MOE_1}{1.645},
\qquad
SE_2 = \frac{MOE_2}{1.645}
\]
Assuming the two estimates are independent, the standard error of the difference is:
\[
SE_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2}
\]
Define the difference as:
\[
\text{Difference} = \text{Estimate}_1 - \text{Estimate}_2
\]
The Z-score is:
\[
Z = \frac{\text{Estimate}_1 - \text{Estimate}2}{SE{\text{diff}}}
\]
The 90% confidence interval for the change is:
\[
\text{Difference} \pm 1.645 \times SE_{\text{diff}}
\]

title: Verify the Claim: Did Philadelphia’s Poverty Rate Change Significantly?
text:
Read the origin report.
I examine whether poverty rates in Philadelphia changed significantly between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS five-year periods. I use census tract estimates from Census Bureau Table B17001, “Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age.” Specifically, I use the population for whom poverty status is determined (B17001_001) as the denominator and the population below the poverty level (B17001_002) as the numerator. The two periods do not overlap.
The following hypothesis is made:
\(\text{H}_0\): The poverty rate in tracts of Philadelphia is not changed from 2010 to 2017.


Show code
library(tidycensus)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(gt)

# H0: The poverty rate in tracts of Philadelphia is not changed from 2010 to 2017.

acs_list <- c("B17001_001", "B17001_002")

format_poverty <- function(df){
  df %>%
  mutate(
    variable = recode(
      variable,
      "B17001_001" = "Total Population",
      "B17001_002" = "Population in Poverty"
    )
  )%>%
    pivot_wider(
      id_cols = c(GEOID, NAME),
      names_from = variable,
      values_from = c(estimate, moe),
      names_glue = "{variable}_{.value}",
      names_vary = "slowest"
    )
}

poverty_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = acs_list,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5"
) %>%
  format_poverty()

poverty_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = acs_list,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5"
) %>%
  format_poverty()

title: Verify the Claim: Did Philadelphia’s Poverty Rate Change Significantly?

Code
The following code provide info for later discussion.


Show code
poverty <- poverty_2010 %>%
  inner_join(
    poverty_2017,
    by = c("GEOID", "NAME"),
    suffix = c("_2010", "_2017")
  )


poverty_withrate <- poverty %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate_2010 =
      `Population in Poverty_estimate_2010` /
      na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2010`, 0),

    poverty_rate_moe_2010 = tidycensus::moe_prop(
      num = `Population in Poverty_estimate_2010`,
      denom = na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2010`, 0),
      moe_num = `Population in Poverty_moe_2010`,
      moe_denom = `Total Population_moe_2010`
    ),

    poverty_rate_2017 =
      `Population in Poverty_estimate_2017` /
      na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2017`, 0),

    poverty_rate_moe_2017 = tidycensus::moe_prop(
      num = `Population in Poverty_estimate_2017`,
      denom = na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2017`, 0),
      moe_num = `Population in Poverty_moe_2017`,
      moe_denom = `Total Population_moe_2017`
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    cv_2010 = poverty_rate_moe_2010 / 1.645 / poverty_rate_2010 * 100,
    cv_2017 = poverty_rate_moe_2017 / 1.645 / poverty_rate_2017 * 100
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    delta_p = poverty_rate_2017 - poverty_rate_2010,
    delta_moe = sqrt(poverty_rate_moe_2010^2 + poverty_rate_moe_2017^2)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    max_p = delta_p + delta_moe,
    min_p = delta_p - delta_moe,
    include_zero = ifelse(min_p <= 0 & max_p >= 0, TRUE, FALSE)
  )




Show code

  arrange(desc(delta_p)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"))

  arrange(delta_p) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"))


ggplot(increase_top_15) +
  geom_col(aes(x = reorder(NAME, delta_p), y = delta_p, fill = include_zero)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = reorder(NAME, delta_p), ymin = min_p, ymax = max_p), width = 0.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = "Census Tract",
    y = "Increase in Poverty Rate (2010-2017)",
    title = "Increase in Poverty Rate in Philadelphia Census Tracts (2010-2017)",
    subtitle = "Top 15, error bars show 90% confidence intervals",
    fill = "Includes Zero"
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed")+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "lightblue", "FALSE" = "salmon")) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Verify the Claim: Did Philadelphia’s Poverty Rate Change Significantly?
text:
Findings
Of the 376 testable census tracts, 36 showed statistically significant increases in poverty rates and 27 showed significant decreases at the 90% confidence level. The remaining 313 showed no statistically detectable change. Eight additional tracts were not testable because their poverty-universe population estimates were zero in at least one period.
